entry.title: Fixing the Front Door
entry.summary: Originally posted October 30, 2026 on elijahpaul.io. TLDR Telegram onboarding has been the biggest pain since launch. We're swapping it out. Meanwhile, the people already inside are building on top of Hot Bot. Lots of people have been approved for days and still see "not approved" when they check through Telegram. We tested it. The likely culprit: connecting Telegram from inside the X app instead of an external browser. The workaround for now: Open the link in an external browser. If that still fails, verify with your wallet instead. Not good enough. So we're replacing the onboarding flow entirely. My words, mid-morning: "it was a bigger pain than we thought it would be." Until the new flow lands, we're in the replies. Approved. Invited. Added to the group. One by one, all day. Team no sleep, but making sure everyone is looked after. Favorite thing about the Hot Bot community: everyone's working together to make it. Strategies. MCP setups. Ideas for new features. Absolute euphoric feeling vs being stranded in the Cold War of the PvP bundlers. One of our users, @0xJohnB, built an anti-rug dashboard that reads his Hot Bot team through our MCP API. Strategies, trades and activity in one view, next to his own anti-rug checks. Read-only by design. Running on a Raspberry Pi 5 at home. That's the point of exposing the stack. Cooking with gas. We push most users to trade on paper first. On purpose. Get a feel for Hot Bot without losing money. Then give us feedback. Subscriptions cover our costs. Proper software business. Whole market was down today. Avg day in crypto. We ride. Long on vision. Relentless on daily execution. 🔥🤖 Elijah Paul, @elijahintek Co-founder of Hot Bot. Scottsdale, AZ God calls us to serve others. I try to live that in business and in life. First posted on elijahpaul.io

entry.title: Your setTimeout Didn't Break — Chrome Killed It
entry.summary:
The log said the sync was scheduled. Two minutes later, nothing had run. No error, no rejected promise, no missed callback warning — just a line that promised future work and a database that never changed. Here is the excerpt that ended a week of blaming my own debounce logic: [10:41:02] change detected [10:41:02] sync scheduled in 120000ms [10:41:32] service worker terminated (idle)
The timer did not fail. The process that owned it was shut down, and a setTimeout cannot outlive its process. The short version setTimeout is a handle in the worker's heap. Terminate the worker and the handle is gone. MV3 kills an idle background worker after about 30 seconds, no matter what is pending. Persist the due time, not the timer, and re-arm it when the worker wakes. The debounce. The code coalesced …

entry.title: Store Timestamps in UTC, Display Them Locally
entry.summary:
A CRM stores '10:30' beside a follow-up task. One representative reads it in Jaipur and another in London. Neither knows which timezone the value represents. Time data needs to describe either an instant or a local scheduling intention. Those are different requirements. An enquiry acceptance time is an instant. Store it using a timezone-aware database type or an explicit UTC representation supported by your system. entry.title: UUIDv4 Is Not Free: Why Random Primary Keys Are Silently Crushing Your Write Performance
entry.summary: When my database write latency spiked by 340% after crossing 50 million rows, my CPU wasn't maxed out. My queries weren't missing indexes. Instead, my storage IOPS was completely saturated by a single architectural default I set up on day one: using UUIDv4 as my primary key. Most backend engineers avoid auto-incrementing integers (BIGINT / SERIAL) in public-facing systems for good reasons. Sequential IDs leak business metrics, enable enumeration attacks (/api/orders/1042, /api/orders/1043), and make distributed ID generation across microservices painful. So I reached for the industry standard: UUIDv4. It is 128 bits of randomness, requires zero coordination between nodes, and guarantees global uniqueness. What looks like a clean architectural win in code review turns into an I/O nightmare…

entry.title: Even a mechanical migration deserves a spec
entry.summary: Swapping Jest for Vitest is a mechanical migration. I still wrote a spec before touching a single test. The reason was simple: the design system already ran on Vite (Storybook included), and Jest with ts-jest kept a second transform pipeline alive just for tests. Consolidate, and get faster. The spec had three parts. Inventory. 68 test files. jest.fn in about 120 places across 30 files. jest.mock in 15. Fake timers in exactly one file. toBeInTheDocument used 219 times. I knew exactly what would break. Non-goals. No migrating legacy packages that have no tests. No root-level Vitest config until a second package gets tests. No swapping jsdom for happy-dom. And no behavior changes in the tests, only jest.* becoming vi.*. Definition of done. All 68 files passing with the same assertions, pnpm test and CI working unchanged, and five dependencies removed: jest, ts-jest, jest-environment-jsdom, @types/jest and ts-node. Result: one day of spec, one day of migration, five small, reviewable commits. The part that protects you most is the non-goals list. A mechanical migration turns into a rewrite the moment someone thinks "while I'm here...". What was the last "simple" migration that grew on your team?
